cloze.text: Chlorhexidine is used after {{c1::scaling and root planing (SRP)}} to reduce bacterial load and promote healing; it is indicated for gingivitis, periodontitis, mucositis and {{c2::peri-implantitis}}.
Topical/local chlorhexidine has no known {{c1::systemic absorption}}, so it is safe during {{c2::pregnancy and breastfeeding}}.
Tuberculosis (TB) is caused by the bacterium {{c1::Mycobacterium tuberculosis}}, which primarily affects the {{c2::lungs}} but can also affect other organs.
Anti-tuberculosis drugs used for long periods include {{c1::isoniazid (INH)}}, {{c2::rifampin}} (Rifadin®) and {{c3::pyrazinamide}} (Pyrazinamide®).
The PPD ({{c1::purified protein derivative}}) test, also called the {{c2::Mantoux}} skin test, injects a small amount of TB antigen just under the skin.
A positive PPD test does NOT mean the patient has {{c1::active TB}}; a {{c2::chest X-ray}} or further tests are required to rule it out.
A virus is much smaller than a fungus or bacterium; it must invade a {{c1::living cell}} and release its {{c2::DNA or RNA}} to reproduce.
Antiviral drugs do not work like antibiotics: they target specific viruses and interfere with {{c1::viral replication (DNA or RNA copying)}}.
{{c1::Acyclovir}} (Zovirax®) treats HSV-1 (cold sores), HSV-2 (genital herpes), {{c2::shingles (varicella-zoster)}} and {{c2::Epstein-Barr virus (mononucleosis)}}.
{{c1::Docosanol}} (Abreva®) is available {{c2::over-the-counter}} and is used for oral herpes labialis (cold sores).
{{c1::Zidovudine}} (AZT®, Retrovir®) is used to manage {{c2::HIV}} infections; it reduces viral load and slows disease progression.
Nystatin (Mycostatin®) is a {{c1::polyene}} antifungal used {{c2::topically}} as a rinse, lozenge or ointment; it is great for localized candidiasis and denture wearers.
Board Alert: nystatin oral suspension can contain {{c1::sugar}} (to improve taste), so patients using it have an increased {{c2::caries}} risk.
cloze.extra: How a drug is delivered matters — tie the delivery form to the oral finding in case studies.

cloze.text: Clotrimazole (Mycelex®) is an {{c1::imidazole}} antifungal used topically as a {{c2::lozenge/troche}}; it is good for compliance because of its pleasant taste.
Fluconazole (Diflucan®) is a {{c1::triazole}} antifungal taken {{c2::systemically}} (oral tablet/suspension); use it if topical therapy fails and monitor for systemic side effects.
cloze.extra: Also used for esophageal or systemic infections.

cloze.text: Ketoconazole is an {{c1::imidazole}} antifungal (systemic oral tablet; topical cream); it is {{c2::not a first choice}} and rarely used in oral candidiasis today — consider alternatives.

Patients using inhaled {{c1::corticosteroids}} (e.g., fluticasone, budesonide) are at increased risk for {{c2::candidiasis}}; always recommend they {{c3::rinse with water and spit}} after inhaler use.
SSRIs ({{c1::selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors}}) work by inhibiting the reuptake of {{c2::serotonin}}; examples are fluoxetine, sertraline and citalopram.
SSRIs are {{c1::first-line}} for depression and anxiety and the most commonly prescribed antidepressants today, because of fewer side effects and safer profiles than older drugs.
cloze.extra: In dentistry patients may take them for depression or anxiety (may be pre-op).

cloze.text: SSRIs: the main dental concern is that {{c1::xerostomia}} is common; drug-interaction risk is {{c2::low}}.
cloze.extra: Common side effects: GI upset, insomnia, dry mouth, headache.

cloze.text: TCAs ({{c1::tricyclic antidepressants}}, e.g., {{c2::amitriptyline}}) inhibit the reuptake of serotonin + {{c3::norepinephrine}}.
cloze.extra: In dentistry sometimes used for chronic pain or anxiety.

cloze.text: TCAs have a {{c1::high}} interaction risk with epinephrine and sedatives; common side effects are dry mouth, drowsiness, dizziness and {{c2::arrhythmia}} risk.
MAOIs ({{c1::monoamine oxidase inhibitors}}, e.g., {{c2::phenelzine}}) inhibit the {{c3::breakdown}} of monoamines (serotonin, norepinephrine, dopamine).

MAOIs are rarely prescribed today because of complex dietary restrictions: combining them with aged cheese, red wine or cured meats can cause {{c1::hypertensive crisis}}; {{c2::epinephrine}} should also be avoided.
cloze.extra: Dental concern: avoid vasoconstrictors, major interaction risk; rare in dentistry. Side effects: orthostatic hypotension, hypertensive crisis.

cloze.text: NDRIs (norepinephrine-dopamine reuptake inhibitors, e.g., {{c1::bupropion}}) inhibit the reuptake of norepinephrine + {{c2::dopamine}}.
Bupropion is used off-label for {{c1::smoking cessation}} and also for ADHD and nicotine withdrawal; its dental concern is possible {{c2::seizure threshold}} reduction.
cloze.extra: Interacts with stimulants. Side effects: dry mouth, anxiety, insomnia.

cloze.text: All antidepressants can cause {{c1::xerostomia}}, which can increase {{c2::caries}} risk and contribute to bad breath and oral discomfort.
Typical antipsychotics are {{c1::first}}-generation agents, e.g., chlorpromazine (Thorazine®) and haloperidol (Haldol®), used for {{c2::schizophrenia}} and acute psychosis.

Atypical antipsychotics are {{c1::second}}-generation agents, e.g., clozapine (Clozaril®), risperidone (Risperdal®), olanzapine (Zyprexa®) and quetiapine (Seroquel®), used for schizophrenia, {{c2::bipolar disorder}} and mood stabilization.

Typical antipsychotics: dental concerns are xerostomia, {{c1::tardive dyskinesia}} and sedation; side effects include sedation, {{c2::EPS}} (tremors, stiffness, muscle spasms, restlessness) and {{c3::orthostatic hypotension}}.
cloze.extra: EPS = extrapyramidal symptoms.

cloze.text: Typical antipsychotics cause increased sedation with {{c1::CNS depressants}}; use caution with {{c2::epinephrine}}.
Atypical antipsychotics: dental concerns are xerostomia and {{c1::metabolic issues (weight gain, diabetes risk)}}; they cause {{c2::less EPS}} than typical agents.
cloze.extra: Side effects: sedation, weight gain. Interactions similar to typical agents; may increase blood glucose.

cloze.text: Benzodiazepines {{c1::enhance GABA}} → CNS depression; examples are diazepam (Valium®), lorazepam (Ativan®) and alprazolam (Xanax®).
Benzodiazepines have a strong {{c1::additive}} effect with CNS depressants; {{c2::short}}-acting agents (e.g., triazolam) are preferred.
Benzodiazepine generic names usually end in {{c1::-pam}} or {{c1::-lam}}.
cloze.extra: WakeUpMemory: "A lam called Pam calms you down."

cloze.text: Non-benzodiazepine hypnotics (sedative-hypnotics, e.g., zolpidem and eszopiclone) selectively enhance {{c1::GABA-A}} receptors and are mainly prescribed for {{c2::sleep}}, not anxiety.
cloze.extra: Interactions: same as benzos.

cloze.text: The beta-blocker {{c1::propranolol}} (Inderal®) blocks {{c2::beta-1}} receptors to reduce heart rate and tremors; it is used for {{c3::situational}} anxiety, not long-term.
cloze.extra: Caution with vasoconstrictors.

cloze.text: {{c1::Buspirone}} (Buspar®), an azapirone, acts by serotonin modulation and is {{c2::non-sedating}}.
SSRIs (e.g., sertraline, paroxetine), originally developed as antidepressants, are now {{c1::first-line}} for chronic generalized anxiety disorder (GAD); they interact with many drugs.
Every antianxiety drug class (benzodiazepines, non-benzo hypnotics, beta blockers, buspirone/SSRIs) lists {{c1::xerostomia}} and drowsiness as side effects.
Anxiety disorders include generalized anxiety disorder (GAD), {{c1::panic disorder}}, phobias, {{c2::OCD}} and social anxiety.
Besides anxiety, benzodiazepines are also used as {{c1::muscle relaxants}}, sedatives and {{c2::anticonvulsants}}.
Alcohol is a {{c1::depressant}}; its oral effects are xerostomia, {{c2::bleeding}} and poor healing.
Opioids are {{c1::depressants}}; their oral effects are xerostomia and {{c2::sedation}}.
Methamphetamine is a {{c1::stimulant}} whose oral effect is "{{c2::meth mouth}}" (caries, attrition, dry mucosa).
Cocaine is a {{c1::stimulant}}; its oral effects are {{c2::mucosal burns}} and vasoconstriction.
Nicotine is a {{c1::stimulant}}; its oral effects are xerostomia, {{c2::staining}} and delayed healing.
Marijuana is classed (in the book) as a {{c1::psychedelic}}; oral effects are xerostomia, anxiety and {{c2::reduced pain control}}.
LSD is a {{c1::psychedelic}}; its effects are hallucinations and {{c2::altered perception}}.
Alcohol: key risk is {{c1::liver damage}} → bleeding risk; dental management is to {{c2::monitor bleeding}} and use caution with trauma.
Opioids: key risks are dependence and {{c1::CNS depression}}; dental management is to {{c2::limit sedation}} and keep appointments short.
Methamphetamine: key risks are severe decay, {{c1::bruxism}} and poor hygiene; dental management is to avoid epinephrine and provide {{c2::fluoride}}.
"Meth mouth" is caused by the drug's {{c1::acidity}}, severe dry mouth, high {{c2::sugar}} intake, clenching/grinding and poor oral hygiene during binges.
Cocaine: key risk is {{c1::cardiac arrest}} with epinephrine; give no epinephrine if cocaine was used in the past {{c2::24}} hours.
cloze.extra: Epinephrine should be carefully considered in any stimulant user (especially cocaine).

cloze.text: Nicotine: key risks are periodontal destruction and {{c1::implant failure}}; dental management is hygiene counseling and {{c2::cessation support}}.
Marijuana: key risk is {{c1::anxiety/paranoia}} during care; dental management is a calm tone and {{c2::adjusting anesthesia}}.
cloze.extra: Substance use (especially cannabis or CNS stimulants) may interfere with anesthetic response and require dose adjustments.

cloze.text: LSD: key risk is disorientation and unpredictable behavior; dental management is to {{c1::postpone care}} during active effects.
Pinpoint pupils ({{c1::miosis}}) are a classic sign of {{c2::opioid}} use or overdose, often with sedation and respiratory depression.
cloze.extra: WakeUpMemory: "MIosis = mini pupils" (e.g., heroin, morphine).

cloze.text: Dilated pupils ({{c1::mydriasis}}) are associated with {{c2::stimulant}} use (cocaine, amphetamines, methamphetamine) and may indicate recent or active use.
cloze.extra: WakeUpMemory: "MYdriasis = my eyes wide!"

cloze.text: When prescribing for recovering addicts, use caution with opioids — {{c1::non-narcotic}} pain control (e.g., NSAIDs, acetaminophen) is preferred.
Anticonvulsants prevent or control seizures and are prescribed off-label for {{c1::neuropathic pain}}, {{c2::trigeminal neuralgia}}, bipolar disorder and fibromyalgia.
{{c1::Phenytoin}} (Dilantin®) binds {{c2::sodium channels}} to stabilize neurons; its major oral side effect is {{c3::gingival hyperplasia}}.
cloze.extra: WakeUpMemory: "Ph" in Phenytoin = Puffy and Hyperplasia → "Phenytoin = Puffy Gums."

cloze.text: {{c1::Carbamazepine}} (Tegretol®) blocks sodium channels and is the drug of choice for {{c2::trigeminal neuralgia}}.
Carbamazepine causes xerostomia and dizziness and may lead to {{c1::leukopenia}}, which can present as delayed healing or {{c2::oral ulcers}}.
Phenobarbital (Luminal®) is a {{c1::barbiturate}} that increases {{c2::GABA}} activity, causing sedation and {{c3::respiratory depression}}.
cloze.extra: Long-term use may affect mental clarity and reduce oral hygiene ability.

cloze.text: {{c1::Gabapentin}} (Neurontin®) and {{c1::pregabalin}} (Lyrica®) are used for neuropathic pain and {{c2::fibromyalgia}}.
cloze.extra: Side effects: dry mouth, drowsiness, incoordination → can impair brushing and increase caries or burning mouth sensation.

cloze.text: Muscle relaxants reduce muscle {{c1::spasms}} from injury, neurologic disorders or chronic pain; most act on the {{c2::central nervous system}} to dampen motor signals.
{{c1::Cyclobenzaprine}} (Flexeril®) relieves skeletal muscle spasms but frequently causes {{c2::xerostomia}}, drowsiness and dizziness.
cloze.extra: Patients may report burning mouth, cracked lips or increased caries risk from reduced saliva.

cloze.text: Methocarbamol (Robaxin®), baclofen and tizanidine are {{c1::CNS depressants}} that reduce muscle tone; they can cause fatigue, {{c2::orthostatic hypotension}} and reduced coordination (affecting brushing).
Antihistamines treat {{c1::mild to moderate}} allergy symptoms (sneezing, hives, rash) by {{c2::blocking histamine}}.
Antihistamines cause xerostomia, dizziness and drowsiness — especially {{c1::diphenhydramine}}.
cloze.extra: Dental tips: advise hydration; monitor for sedation or dizziness during long appointments.

cloze.text: Epinephrine (EpiPen®) is the emergency treatment for {{c1::anaphylaxis}}: it opens airways and {{c2::raises blood pressure}} quickly.
cloze.extra: Side effects: mild xerostomia, rapid heartbeat, anxiety, tremors. Dental tip: confirm EpiPen use if allergy is known; record medical history clearly.

cloze.text: Corticosteroids (e.g., fluticasone, hydrocortisone, prednisone) treat chronic allergy conditions (rhinitis, eczema, asthma) by {{c1::suppressing the immune response}} to reduce inflammation.
Corticosteroid side effects include xerostomia, {{c1::delayed healing}}, infection risk and {{c2::osteoporosis}} (with long-term use).
cloze.extra: Dental tip: ask about long-term use — healing and infection risk increase with systemic steroids.

cloze.text: Leukotriene receptor antagonists (e.g., {{c1::montelukast}}) are used for long-term allergy and {{c2::asthma}} management; they block leukotrienes, chemicals that trigger swelling and mucus.
cloze.extra: Side effects: headache, possible mood or sleep changes. No emergency dental concerns — confirm other allergy medications used.

cloze.text: An allergic reaction occurs when the immune system overreacts to an {{c1::antigen}} (foreign substance).
Immunosuppressants suppress the immune system to prevent {{c1::rejection of transplanted organs}} and to manage {{c2::autoimmune}} diseases.
The major oral side effect of {{c1::cyclosporine}} (Sandimmune®) is {{c2::gingival hyperplasia}}, especially with poor plaque control.
cloze.extra: Cause: stimulated fibroblasts and altered collagen metabolism (same mechanism as phenytoin).

cloze.text: Type I diabetes is {{c1::autoimmune destruction}} of pancreatic {{c2::β-cells}}, so the body produces little or no insulin.
Type I diabetes is treated primarily with {{c1::insulin injections or an insulin pump}}; drug classes are insulin and {{c2::amylin analogues}}.
In Type II diabetes the body becomes {{c1::resistant to insulin}} or doesn't produce enough; it is often linked to obesity and lifestyle.
Type II diabetes is treated primarily with {{c1::oral medications}} (e.g., metformin), lifestyle changes, and sometimes insulin.
Type II diabetes drug classes include biguanides, {{c1::sulfonylureas}}, meglitinides, {{c2::GLP-1 agonists}}, DPP-4 inhibitors and SGLT2 inhibitors.

basic.front: Why can chlorhexidine be used long term (e.g., peri-implantitis management) when antibiotics should not be?
basic.back: Chlorhexidine does not cause bacterial resistance (unlike antibiotics). Its cosmetic side effects (staining, taste) are what limit extended use.

basic.front: Why does TB treatment require multiple drugs taken over many months?
basic.back: Because of the bacteria's resistance and slow replication rate.

basic.front: Why are viral infections harder to treat than bacterial infections?
basic.back: The virus lives inside the host's cells, so it is hard for drugs to target it without harming the body.

basic.front: How should a patient use nystatin rinse?
basic.back: Hold the rinse in the mouth before spitting, and remove dentures before use.

basic.front: What do you tell a patient about taking a clotrimazole troche?
basic.back: Let the troche dissolve slowly — do not chew or swallow it.

basic.front: Why is epinephrine (vasoconstrictor) avoided in local anesthetic for patients taking TCAs?
basic.back: TCAs can amplify the cardiovascular effects of epinephrine, potentially leading to hypertensive crisis — so the book says epinephrine is generally contraindicated in local anesthetics for these patients.
basic.extra: Dental concerns for TCAs: xerostomia, drowsiness, avoid epinephrine.

basic.back: Involuntary oral/facial movements — a dental concern with typical antipsychotics

basic.front: What causes phenytoin-induced gingival hyperplasia, and how does the hygienist manage it?
basic.back: Stimulation of fibroblasts and altered collagen metabolism — worst with poor plaque control. Emphasize meticulous brushing and regular dental visits.

basic.front: What precautions does the hygienist take for a patient on muscle relaxants?
basic.back: Ask whether she took the medication before arriving (it may impair driving); recline and raise the chair slowly to avoid dizziness/fainting; reinforce basic hygiene routines and recommend frequent hydration for dry mouth.

basic.front: Why coordinate with the physician before surgical or invasive procedures on a patient taking immunosuppressants?
basic.back: These patients are more susceptible to infection and may have delayed healing.

typein.question: TB treatment with multiple drugs usually lasts how many months? (format: x–y)
A PPD (Mantoux) skin test is read how many hours after injection? (format: x–y)
typein.extra: The swelling at the injection site is read.

typein.question: Antifungal treatment for oral candidiasis usually lasts how many days? (format: x–y)
typein.extra: May be extended for immunocompromised patients or recurrent infections.

typein.question: Antidepressants usually take how many weeks to take effect? (format: x–y)
typein.extra: Onset is slow — not a "quick fix."

mcq.question: A new patient reports that her PPD (Mantoux) skin test read positive at 48 hours last week. Which statement is most accurate?
options: A. She has active, infectious tuberculosis
B. She needs a chest X-ray or further tests to rule out active TB
C. The test must be repeated because it should be read at 24 hours
D. She should begin a 7–14 day course of isoniazid
mcq.answer: B. She needs a chest X-ray or further tests to rule out active TB
mcq.explanation: A positive PPD shows exposure/response to the TB antigen, not active disease; a chest X-ray or further tests rule out active TB. It is read at 48–72 hours (so 48 h is valid), and TB treatment lasts 6–9 months with multiple drugs, not 7–14 days.

mcq.question: A denture wearer has used nystatin oral suspension for several weeks for denture stomatitis. At recall she has new root caries. Which is the most likely drug-related reason?
options: B. The oral suspension can contain sugar
C. Nystatin is a systemic triazole that alters saliva
D. Nystatin stains and demineralizes root surfaces
mcq.answer: B. The oral suspension can contain sugar
mcq.explanation: Nystatin oral suspension can contain sugar to improve taste, raising caries risk (Board Alert). Nystatin is a topical polyene, not a systemic triazole (that is fluconazole).

mcq.question: A patient taking amitriptyline for chronic facial pain needs quadrant scaling with local anesthesia. Which is the greatest pharmacologic concern?
options: A. Increased bleeding from platelet inhibition
B. Amplified cardiovascular effects of epinephrine, risking hypertensive crisis
mcq.answer: B. Amplified cardiovascular effects of epinephrine, risking hypertensive crisis
mcq.explanation: Amitriptyline is a TCA; TCAs amplify the cardiovascular effects of epinephrine (possible hypertensive crisis), so the vasoconstrictor is avoided. Lowered seizure threshold is the concern for bupropion (NDRI), not TCAs.

mcq.question: Which patient-reported medication should make the clinician ask about aged cheese, red wine and cured meats, and avoid epinephrine?
mcq.explanation: Phenelzine is an MAOI: MAOIs with aged cheese, red wine or cured meats can cause hypertensive crisis, and epinephrine should be avoided. Sertraline and fluoxetine are SSRIs with low interaction risk.

mcq.question: A patient with schizophrenia who has taken haloperidol for years shows repetitive lip-smacking and tongue movements she cannot control. This is most likely:
mcq.explanation: Haloperidol is a typical (first-generation) antipsychotic; tardive dyskinesia = involuntary oral/facial movements. Orthostatic hypotension is also a side effect but causes dizziness on standing, not oral movements.

mcq.question: A patient with chronic generalized anxiety asks for an antianxiety medication that will not make her sleepy. Which agent from the book fits best?
mcq.explanation: Buspirone (azapirone) is non-sedating. Alprazolam and diazepam are benzodiazepines (GABA → CNS depression) and zolpidem is a sedative-hypnotic for sleep.

mcq.question: A patient arrives with dilated pupils, is talkative and jittery, and admits to using cocaine this morning. She needs local anesthesia for scaling. Best management?
options: A. Use lidocaine with 1:100,000 epinephrine as usual
B. Avoid epinephrine — none if cocaine was used in the past 24 hours
C. Give extra epinephrine to overcome reduced anesthetic response
D. Prescribe an opioid for post-op pain
mcq.answer: B. Avoid epinephrine — none if cocaine was used in the past 24 hours
mcq.explanation: Cocaine plus epinephrine carries a risk of cardiac arrest; no epinephrine if used within 24 hours. Dilated pupils (mydriasis) fit stimulant use; opioids are not a fix here and are cautioned in substance users.

mcq.question: A patient with a seizure disorder presents with generalized, firm gingival overgrowth that is worse where plaque control is poor. Which medication is most likely responsible?
mcq.explanation: Phenytoin (Dilantin) causes gingival hyperplasia via fibroblast stimulation and altered collagen metabolism, worse with poor plaque control. Carbamazepine also treats seizures but its oral risks are xerostomia and leukopenia (ulcers, delayed healing).

mcq.question: Two years after a kidney transplant, a patient presents with fibrous gingival enlargement and heavy plaque. Which drug on her medication list is the most likely cause?
mcq.explanation: Cyclosporine (an immunosuppressant used to prevent transplant rejection) causes gingival hyperplasia, especially with poor plaque control. Prednisone (corticosteroid) causes delayed healing, infection risk and osteoporosis, not gingival overgrowth.
